claim: G6b-B is critical for platelet production and activation.
source: The immunoreceptor tyrosine-based inhibition motif (ITIM)-containing receptor G6b-B is critical for platelet production and activation.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract as a summary of the receptor's function.

claim: Loss of G6b-B results in severe macrothrombocytopenia in mice and humans.
source: Loss of G6b-B results in severe macrothrombocytopenia, myelofibrosis and aberrant platelet function in mice and humans.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by references to previous studies.

claim: Loss of G6b-B results in myelofibrosis in mice and humans.
source: Loss of G6b-B results in severe macrothrombocytopenia, myelofibrosis and aberrant platelet function in mice and humans.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by references to previous studies.

claim: Loss of G6b-B results in aberrant platelet function in mice and humans.
source: Loss of G6b-B results in severe macrothrombocytopenia, myelofibrosis and aberrant platelet function in mice and humans.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by references to previous studies.

claim: Perlecan was identified as a G6b-B binding partner using immunohistochemistry, affinity chromatography and proteomics.
source: Using a combination of immunohistochemistry, affinity chromatography and proteomics, we identified the extracellular matrix heparan sulfate (HS) proteoglycan perlecan as a G6b-B binding partner.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data in the results section.

claim: The interaction between G6b-B and perlecan is specifically mediated by the HS chains of perlecan.
source: Subsequent in vitro biochemical studies and a cell-based genetic screen demonstrated that the interaction is specifically mediated by the HS chains of perlecan.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data including heparinase treatment and CRISPR screening.

claim: Heparin forms a high-affinity complex with G6b-B.
source: Biophysical analysis revealed that heparin forms a high-affinity complex with G6b-B and mediates dimerization.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by SPR and size exclusion chromatography data.

claim: Heparin mediates G6b-B dimerization.
source: Biophysical analysis revealed that heparin forms a high-affinity complex with G6b-B and mediates dimerization.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by size exclusion chromatography and crystallography data.

claim: Binding of G6b-B to HS and multivalent heparin inhibits platelet function.
source: Using platelets from humans and genetically modified mice, we demonstrate that binding of G6b-B to HS and multivalent heparin inhibits platelet and megakaryocyte function by inducing downstream signaling via the tyrosine phosphatases Shp1 and Shp2.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by platelet adhesion and aggregation assays.

claim: Binding of G6b-B to HS and multivalent heparin inhibits megakaryocyte function.
source: Using platelets from humans and genetically modified mice, we demonstrate that binding of G6b-B to HS and multivalent heparin inhibits platelet and megakaryocyte function by inducing downstream signaling via the tyrosine phosphatases Shp1 and Shp2.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by megakaryocyte adhesion assays.

claim: G6b-B inhibits platelet and megakaryocyte function by inducing downstream signaling via Shp1.
source: Using platelets from humans and genetically modified mice, we demonstrate that binding of G6b-B to HS and multivalent heparin inhibits platelet and megakaryocyte function by inducing downstream signaling via the tyrosine phosphatases Shp1 and Shp2.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by Western blot data showing Shp1 phosphorylation.

claim: G6b-B inhibits platelet and megakaryocyte function by inducing downstream signaling via Shp2.
source: Using platelets from humans and genetically modified mice, we demonstrate that binding of G6b-B to HS and multivalent heparin inhibits platelet and megakaryocyte function by inducing downstream signaling via the tyrosine phosphatases Shp1 and Shp2.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by Western blot data showing Shp2 phosphorylation.

claim: Platelets are anucleated cell fragments produced by megakaryocytes in the bone marrow, spleen and lungs.
source: Platelets are highly reactive anucleated cell fragments, which are produced by megakaryocytes (MKs) in the bone marrow, spleen and lungs.
evidence: This is a statement of established knowledge in the introduction.

claim: Platelets circulate in the blood stream for 7–10 days.
source: In an intact vasculature, platelets circulate in the blood stream for 7–10 days and are finally cleared by the reticulo-endothelial system in the spleen and liver.
evidence: This is a statement of established knowledge in the introduction.

claim: Platelets are cleared by the reticulo-endothelial system in the spleen and liver.
source: In an intact vasculature, platelets circulate in the blood stream for 7–10 days and are finally cleared by the reticulo-endothelial system in the spleen and liver.
evidence: This is a statement of established knowledge in the introduction.

claim: Upon vascular injury, platelets adhere to the exposed vascular extracellular matrix.
source: Upon vascular injury, however, platelets adhere to the exposed vascular extracellular matrix (ECM), become activated and form a hemostatic plug that seals the wound.
evidence: This is a statement of established knowledge in the introduction.

claim: Platelet activation must be tightly regulated to avoid hyperactivity and indiscriminate vessel occlusion.
source: Platelet activation must be tightly regulated to avoid hyperactivity and indiscriminate vessel occlusion (Bye et al., 2016; Jackson, 2011).
evidence: This is a statement supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Mechanisms that inhibit platelet activation include extrinsic factors such as endothelial-derived nitric oxide and prostacyclin.
source: The mechanisms that inhibit platelet activation include extrinsic factors, such as endothelial-derived nitric oxide and prostacyclin, and intrinsic factors, such as immunoreceptor tyrosine-based inhibition motif (ITIM)-containing receptors (Coxon et al., 2017; Nagy and Smolenski, 2018).
evidence: This is a statement supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Mechanisms that inhibit platelet activation include intrinsic factors such as ITIM-containing receptors.
source: The mechanisms that inhibit platelet activation include extrinsic factors, such as endothelial-derived nitric oxide and prostacyclin, and intrinsic factors, such as immunoreceptor tyrosine-based inhibition motif (ITIM)-containing receptors (Coxon et al., 2017; Nagy and Smolenski, 2018).
evidence: This is a statement supported by citations to previous work.

claim: G6b-B is a unique platelet ITIM-containing receptor.
source: G6b-B is a unique platelet ITIM-containing receptor that is highly expressed in mature MKs and platelets (Coxon et al., 2017; Senis et al., 2007).
evidence: This is a statement supported by citations to previous work.

claim: G6b-B is highly expressed in mature MKs and platelets.
source: G6b-B is a unique platelet ITIM-containing receptor that is highly expressed in mature MKs and platelets (Coxon et al., 2017; Senis et al., 2007).
evidence: This is a statement supported by citations to previous work.

claim: G6b-B is a type I transmembrane protein.
source: It is a type I transmembrane protein that consists of a single N-glycosylated immunoglobulin-variable (IgV)-like domain in its extracellular region, a single transmembrane domain and a cytoplasmic tail containing an ITIM and an immunoreceptor tyrosine-based switch motif (ITSM).
evidence: This is a statement of established knowledge about G6b-B structure.

claim: G6b-B consists of a single N-glycosylated immunoglobulin-variable (IgV)-like domain in its extracellular region.
source: It is a type I transmembrane protein that consists of a single N-glycosylated immunoglobulin-variable (IgV)-like domain in its extracellular region, a single transmembrane domain and a cytoplasmic tail containing an ITIM and an immunoreceptor tyrosine-based switch motif (ITSM).
evidence: This is a statement of established knowledge about G6b-B structure.

claim: G6b-B has a cytoplasmic tail containing an ITIM and an ITSM.
source: It is a type I transmembrane protein that consists of a single N-glycosylated immunoglobulin-variable (IgV)-like domain in its extracellular region, a single transmembrane domain and a cytoplasmic tail containing an ITIM and an immunoreceptor tyrosine-based switch motif (ITSM).
evidence: This is a statement of established knowledge about G6b-B structure.

claim: The central tyrosine residues in the ITIM and ITSM of G6b-B become phosphorylated by Src family kinases.
source: The central tyrosine residues embedded in the consensus sequences of the ITIM ([I/V/L]xYxx[V/L]) and ITSM ([T]xYxx[V/I]) become phosphorylated by Src family kinases (SFKs) and subsequently act as docking sites for the Src homology 2 (SH2) domain-containing protein-tyrosine phosphatases (Shp)1 and 2 (Mazharian et al., 2012; Senis et al., 2007).
evidence: This is a statement supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Phosphorylated tyrosine residues in the ITIM and ITSM of G6b-B act as docking sites for Shp1 and Shp2.
source: The central tyrosine residues embedded in the consensus sequences of the ITIM ([I/V/L]xYxx[V/L]) and ITSM ([T]xYxx[V/I]) become phosphorylated by Src family kinases (SFKs) and subsequently act as docking sites for the Src homology 2 (SH2) domain-containing protein-tyrosine phosphatases (Shp)1 and 2 (Mazharian et al., 2012; Senis et al., 2007).
evidence: This is a statement supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The inhibitory function of G6b-B has been demonstrated in a heterologous cell system.
source: The inhibitory function of G6b-B has been demonstrated in a heterologous cell system, by antibody-mediated crosslinking of the receptor in platelets and G6b-B knockout (KO) mouse models (Mazharian et al., 2012; Mori et al., 2008; Newland et al., 2007).
evidence: This is a statement supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The inhibitory function of G6b-B has been demonstrated by antibody-mediated crosslinking of the receptor in platelets.
source: The inhibitory function of G6b-B has been demonstrated in a heterologous cell system, by antibody-mediated crosslinking of the receptor in platelets and G6b-B knockout (KO) mouse models (Mazharian et al., 2012; Mori et al., 2008; Newland et al., 2007).
evidence: This is a statement supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The inhibitory function of G6b-B has been demonstrated in G6b-B knockout mouse models.
source: The inhibitory function of G6b-B has been demonstrated in a heterologous cell system, by antibody-mediated crosslinking of the receptor in platelets and G6b-B knockout (KO) mouse models (Mazharian et al., 2012; Mori et al., 2008; Newland et al., 2007).
evidence: This is a statement supported by citations to previous work.

claim: G6b-B knockout mice develop severe macrothrombocytopenia.
source: These mice develop a severe macrothrombocytopenia, myelofibrosis, and aberrant megakaryocyte and platelet function, establishing G6b-B as a critical regulator of platelet activation and production.
evidence: This is a statement supported by citations to previous work.

claim: G6b-B knockout mice develop myelofibrosis.
source: These mice develop a severe macrothrombocytopenia, myelofibrosis, and aberrant megakaryocyte and platelet function, establishing G6b-B as a critical regulator of platelet activation and production.
evidence: This is a statement supported by citations to previous work.

claim: G6b-B knockout mice develop aberrant megakaryocyte and platelet function.
source: These mice develop a severe macrothrombocytopenia, myelofibrosis, and aberrant megakaryocyte and platelet function, establishing G6b-B as a critical regulator of platelet activation and production.
evidence: This is a statement supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The phenotype of G6b-B knockout mice was also observed in a G6b-B loss-of-function mouse model (Mpig6bdiYF).
source: This phenotype was also observed in a G6b-B loss-of-function mouse model (Mpig6bdiYF) in which the tyrosine residues within the ITIM and ITSM were mutated to phenylalanine residues, abrogating the binding of Shp1 and Shp2 to G6b-B and downstream signaling (Geer et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a statement supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Expression of human G6b-B in mouse platelets rescued the phenotype of G6b-B-deficient mice.
source: Moreover, expression of human G6b-B in mouse platelets rescued the phenotype of G6b-B-deficient mice, demonstrating that human and mouse G6b-B exert the same physiological functions (Hofmann et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a statement supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Human and mouse G6b-B exert the same physiological functions.
source: Moreover, expression of human G6b-B in mouse platelets rescued the phenotype of G6b-B-deficient mice, demonstrating that human and mouse G6b-B exert the same physiological functions (Hofmann et al., 2018).
evidence: This is inferred from the rescue experiment cited.

claim: Null and loss-of-function mutations in human G6b-B recapitulate key features of the Mpig6b KO and loss-of-function mouse phenotypes.
source: Importantly, null and loss-of-function mutations in human G6b-B have been reported to recapitulate key features of the Mpig6b KO and loss-of-function mouse phenotypes, including a severe macrothrombocytopenia, MK clusters in the bone marrow and myelofibrosis (Hofmann et al., 2018; Melhem et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a statement supported by citations to previous work.

claim: A previous study demonstrated that G6b-B binds to the glycosaminoglycan heparin.
source: Although a previous study demonstrated that G6b-B binds to the glycosaminoglycan (GAG) heparin, the functional significance of this interaction was not known (de Vet et al., 2005).
evidence: This is a statement supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Heparan sulfates are a specific subgroup of GAGs defined by their basic disaccharide unit.
source: Heparan sulfates (HS) are a specific subgroup of GAGs, defined by their basic disaccharide unit.
evidence: This is a statement of established knowledge.

claim: Heparan sulfates are structurally related to heparin.
source: They are structurally related to heparin, which is produced as a macromolecular proteoglycan by tissue-resident mast cells (Lassila et al., 1997) and which, following chemical or enzymatic processing, serves as an anti-coagulant (Chandarajoti et al., 2016; Meneghetti et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a statement of established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Heparin is produced as a macromolecular proteoglycan by tissue-resident mast cells.
source: They are structurally related to heparin, which is produced as a macromolecular proteoglycan by tissue-resident mast cells (Lassila et al., 1997) and which, following chemical or enzymatic processing, serves as an anti-coagulant (Chandarajoti et al., 2016; Meneghetti et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a statement of established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Heparin serves as an anti-coagulant following chemical or enzymatic processing.
source: They are structurally related to heparin, which is produced as a macromolecular proteoglycan by tissue-resident mast cells (Lassila et al., 1997) and which, following chemical or enzymatic processing, serves as an anti-coagulant (Chandarajoti et al., 2016; Meneghetti et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a statement of established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Perlecan is one of the best studied and abundant HS proteoglycans.
source: One of the best studied and abundant HS proteoglycans is perlecan, which is synthesized and secreted by endothelial and smooth muscle cells into the vessel wall.
evidence: This is a statement of established knowledge.

claim: Perlecan is synthesized and secreted by endothelial and smooth muscle cells into the vessel wall.
source: One of the best studied and abundant HS proteoglycans is perlecan, which is synthesized and secreted by endothelial and smooth muscle cells into the vessel wall.
evidence: This is a statement of established knowledge.

claim: Perlecan is comprised of a large 400-kDa core protein and has three HS chains attached to its N-terminus.
source: It is comprised of a large 400-kDa core protein and has three HS chains attached to its N-terminus.
evidence: This is a statement of established knowledge.

claim: A number of proteins reportedly interact with the HS chains and protein core of perlecan.
source: A number of proteins reportedly interact with the HS chains and protein core of perlecan, among them are structural components of the ECM, including laminin, collagen IV and fibronectin, and fibroblast growth factor-2 (Nugent et al., 2000; Whitelock et al., 2008).
evidence: This is a statement supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The proteolytically released C-terminal fragment of perlecan, called endorepellin, binds to integrin α2β1.
source: Of note, the proteolytically released C-terminal fragment of perlecan, called endorepellin, binds to integrin α2β1 and enhances collagen-mediated platelet activation (Bix et al., 2007).
evidence: This is a statement supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Endorepellin enhances collagen-mediated platelet activation.
source: Of note, the proteolytically released C-terminal fragment of perlecan, called endorepellin, binds to integrin α2β1 and enhances collagen-mediated platelet activation (Bix et al., 2007).
evidence: This is a statement supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Perlecan has been shown to exert anti-thrombotic properties in an ovine vascular graft model through its HS side-chains.
source: Perlecan has also been shown to exert anti-thrombotic properties in an ovine vascular graft model through its HS side-chains, although the underlying mechanism has not been defined (Lord et al., 2009).
evidence: This is a statement supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: mG6b-B-Fc stained large vessels including the vena cava and aorta in frozen mouse tissue sections.
source: We consistently observed prominent staining in large vessels, including the vena cava and aorta, and also in smaller vessels in the liver and spleen, that were not observed with the negative control (IgG-Fc) (Figure 1), suggesting the presence of G6b-B ligand in vessel walls.
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 1.

claim: mG6b-B-Fc stained smaller vessels in the liver and spleen in frozen mouse tissue sections.
source: We consistently observed prominent staining in large vessels, including the vena cava and aorta, and also in smaller vessels in the liver and spleen, that were not observed with the negative control (IgG-Fc) (Figure 1), suggesting the presence of G6b-B ligand in vessel walls.
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 1.

claim: The staining pattern of mG6b-B-Fc suggests the presence of G6b-B ligand in vessel walls.
source: We consistently observed prominent staining in large vessels, including the vena cava and aorta, and also in smaller vessels in the liver and spleen, that were not observed with the negative control (IgG-Fc) (Figure 1), suggesting the presence of G6b-B ligand in vessel walls.
evidence: This is an inference based on the staining pattern observed in Figure 1.

claim: Bone marrow sections showed diffuse staining with mG6b-B-Fc, indicative of the presence of the ligand in the bone marrow ECM.
source: The highly vascularized bone marrow sections showed a more diffuse staining, indicative of the presence of the ligand in the bone marrow ECM (Figure 1).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 1.

claim: Mass spectrometry revealed perlecan as the most abundant protein specifically pulled-down with mG6b-B-Fc from vena cava homogenates.
source: Bands were excised and proteins identified by mass spectrometry, revealing basal membrane-specific HS proteoglycan (HSPG) core protein or perlecan as the most abundant protein specifically pulled-down with mG6b-B-Fc (Table 1).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Table 1 and Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: mG6b-B-Fc bound robustly to perlecan in an in vitro binding assay.
source: mG6b-B-Fc bound robustly to perlecan, but not to bovine serum albumin (BSA) (control) or other ECM molecules, including collagen I and IV, various forms of laminin (111, 411, 421, 511 and 521), fibronectin or the related and recombinantly expressed HSPGs syndecan-2 or agrin (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 2A.

claim: mG6b-B-Fc did not bind to BSA, collagen I and IV, various forms of laminin, fibronectin, syndecan-2 or agrin in an in vitro binding assay.
source: mG6b-B-Fc bound robustly to perlecan, but not to bovine serum albumin (BSA) (control) or other ECM molecules, including collagen I and IV, various forms of laminin (111, 411, 421, 511 and 521), fibronectin or the related and recombinantly expressed HSPGs syndecan-2 or agrin (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Human G6b-B-Fc showed binding characteristics similar to those of mG6b-B-Fc.
source: Human G6b-B-Fc (huG6b-B-Fc) showed binding characteristics similar to those of mG6b-B-Fc (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Treatment of perlecan with heparinase III significantly reduced G6b-B binding to immobilized perlecan.
source: Treatment of perlecan with the enzyme heparinase III, which removes the HS side-chains, significantly reduced G6b-B binding to immobilized perlecan (Figure 2B), indicating that G6b-B binds to the HS side-chains rather than the protein core.
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 2B.

claim: G6b-B binds to the HS side-chains of perlecan rather than the protein core.
source: Treatment of perlecan with the enzyme heparinase III, which removes the HS side-chains, significantly reduced G6b-B binding to immobilized perlecan (Figure 2B), indicating that G6b-B binds to the HS side-chains rather than the protein core.
evidence: This is inferred from the heparinase III treatment experiment shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The addition of soluble HS inhibited the binding of G6b-B to immobilized perlecan.
source: This observation was further supported by a competition assay, in which the addition of soluble HS inhibited the binding of G6b-B to immobilized perlecan (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Unfractionated heparin interfered with G6b-B binding to perlecan.
source: Of note, unfractionated heparin, which is closely related to HS, also interfered with G6b-B binding to perlecan and streptavidin-immobilized biotin-conjugated heparin and also bound directly to G6b-B-Fc (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 2A and 2C.

claim: Unfractionated heparin bound directly to G6b-B-Fc.
source: Of note, unfractionated heparin, which is closely related to HS, also interfered with G6b-B binding to perlecan and streptavidin-immobilized biotin-conjugated heparin and also bound directly to G6b-B-Fc (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Only oligomers of at least eight saccharides were able to block binding of G6b-B to heparin-biotin partially.
source: In a competition assay, only oligomers of at least eight saccharides were able to block binding of G6b-B to heparin-biotin partially, suggesting that this is the minimum length required for this interaction (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: High sulfation of the glycan was found to be important for G6b-B binding.
source: In addition, high sulfation of the glycan was found to be important for G6b-B binding, as a loss of occupancy of one sulfation site resulted in a significant drop in the ability of the oligomer to block G6b-B binding to native heparin (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: A genome-wide mutant cell library was generated by transducing Cas9-expressing HEK293 cells with a library of lentiviruses encoding gRNAs targeting 18,009 human genes.
source: A genome-wide mutant cell library was generated by transducing Cas9-expressing HEK293 cells with a library of lentiviruses, each encoding a single gRNA from a pool of 90,709 individual gRNAs targeting 18,009 human genes (Sharma et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the results.

claim: The CRISPR screen identified many genes that are required for HS biosynthesis.
source: Using this strategy, we unambiguously identified many genes that are required for HS biosynthesis, beginning with the generation of the tetrasaccharide linkage on the serine residue of the protein backbone (B3GAT3, XYLT2, B4GALT7), the commitment towards the HS pathway (EXTL3), HS chain polymerization (EXT1/2), and HS chain modification (NDST1, HS2ST1) (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Genes encoding enzymes essential for chondroitin sulfate biosynthesis were not identified in the CRISPR screen.
source: Of particular note, genes encoding the enzymes chondroitin sulfate N-acetylgalactosaminyltransferase 1 and 2 (CSGALNACT1/2), which are essential for the commitment towards the biosynthesis of chondroitin sulfate chains, were not identified, demonstrating that G6b-B binding to HEK293 cells is mediated by HS, but not by chondroitin sulfate (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 3B.

claim: G6b-B binding to HEK293 cells is mediated by HS, but not by chondroitin sulfate.
source: Of particular note, genes encoding the enzymes chondroitin sulfate N-acetylgalactosaminyltransferase 1 and 2 (CSGALNACT1/2), which are essential for the commitment towards the biosynthesis of chondroitin sulfate chains, were not identified, demonstrating that G6b-B binding to HEK293 cells is mediated by HS, but not by chondroitin sulfate (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is inferred from the absence of chondroitin sulfate biosynthesis genes in the CRISPR screen results shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The addition of heparin inhibited G6b-B binding to HEK293 cells.
source: Moreover, the addition of heparin, but not chondroitin sulfate, inhibited G6b-B binding to HEK293 cells (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The addition of chondroitin sulfate did not inhibit G6b-B binding to HEK293 cells.
source: Moreover, the addition of heparin, but not chondroitin sulfate, inhibited G6b-B binding to HEK293 cells (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Targeting SLC35B2 led to a loss of G6b-B binding relative to the parental cell line.
source: We validated the involvement of sulfated HSs in mediating G6b-B binding to cells by individually targeting SLC35B2 and were able to demonstrate that this led to a loss of G6b-B binding relative to the parental cell line (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 3D.

claim: The extracellular domain of G6b-B is enriched in positively charged residues, especially arginines.
source: The extracellular domain of G6b-B is enriched in positively charged residues, especially arginines (12 in 125 amino acids; 9.6% vs 5.6% average frequency in mammalian membrane proteins [Gaur, 2014]), which are known to mediate strong binding to heparin (Margalit et al., 1993).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by citations.

claim: A structural model of G6b-B showed four basic residues (Lys54, Lys58, Arg60 and Arg61) in close spatial proximity to each other on a solvent-exposed loop.
source: Examination of the model showed four basic residues (Lys54, Lys58, Arg60 and Arg61) in close spatial proximity to each other on a solvent-exposed loop.
evidence: This is stated in the results based on a structural model.

claim: Cells expressing mutant G6b-B (K54D, K58D, R60E, R61E) showed impaired heparin binding compared to WT G6b-B expressing cells.
source: Cells expressing WT G6b-B showed an increase in heparin binding compared to that in non-transfected cells, whereas the cells expressing mutant G6b-B showed impaired binding when compared to WT G6b-B expressing cells, demonstrating that these amino acids (or a subset thereof) are involved in ligand binding (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C.

claim: The crystal structure of the G6b-B ECD–dp12–Fab complex was determined to 3.1 Å resolution.
source: Subsequent to the tertiary structure prediction, we were able to generate crystals of the ternary complex of the ectodomain of G6b-B bound to the heparin oligosaccharide dp12, scaffolded by a G6b-B-specific Fab fragment, and we determined the structure of this complex by X-ray crystallography to 3.1 Å resolution (Figure 4 and Table 2).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 4 and Table 2.

claim: The ectodomain of G6b-B forms an immunoglobulin-like fold of a topology closely resembling the structure of a variable immunoglobulin domain.
source: Confirming the fold of the predicted model, the ectodomain of G6b-B forms an immunoglobulin-like fold of a topology closely resembling the structure of a variable immunoglobulin (Ig) domain (Figure 4C) (Brändén and Tooze, 2009).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 4C.

claim: A disulfide bond between cysteine residues 35 and 108 stabilizes the immunoglobulin fold of G6b-B.
source: A disulfide bond between cysteine residues 35 and 108 (strands B and F, respectively) stabilizes the immunoglobulin (Ig) fold (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The ectodomain of G6b-B assembles into an apparent dimer with a pseudo two-fold symmetry.
source: The ectodomain of G6b-B assembles into an apparent dimer with a pseudo two-fold symmetry oriented perpendicular to the extended β-sheet that forms the heparin binding site (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Dimer formation of G6b-B is driven by the heparin ligand.
source: Dimer formation of G6b-B is driven by the heparin ligand, as demonstrated by size exclusion chromatography (Figure 5).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 5.

claim: G6b ECD was eluted at approximately 12.9 kDa in size exclusion chromatography, matching the molecular weight of the monomeric protein.
source: Although G6b ECD was eluted at approximately 12.9 kDa, matching the molecular weight of the monomeric protein, the addition of the heparin oligomer dp12 (3.6 kDa) resulted in a complex of around 30.8 kDa, corresponding to the weight of two G6b-B molecules and one dp12 molecule (Figure 5).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 5.

claim: The addition of dp12 to G6b ECD resulted in a complex of around 30.8 kDa, corresponding to the weight of two G6b-B molecules and one dp12 molecule.
source: Although G6b ECD was eluted at approximately 12.9 kDa, matching the molecular weight of the monomeric protein, the addition of the heparin oligomer dp12 (3.6 kDa) resulted in a complex of around 30.8 kDa, corresponding to the weight of two G6b-B molecules and one dp12 molecule (Figure 5).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 5.

claim: The interface between G6b-B chains E and F buries approximately 800 Å2 of solvent accessible surface area.
source: The interface between chains E and F buries approximately 800 Å2 of solvent accessible surface area.
evidence: This is stated in the results based on structural analysis.

claim: The interface analysis using the PISA software does not predict a stable complex for the G6b-B dimer.
source: In line with the modest surface area buried between the two subunits, the interface analysis using the PISA software does not predict a stable complex (Krissinel and Henrick, 2007), consistent with the observation that ectodomain dimerization is induced by the heparin ligand.
evidence: This is stated in the results based on computational analysis.

claim: Dimerization of G6b-B creates a deep cleft into which the heparin ligand inserts.
source: Nevertheless, dimerization creates a deep cleft, into which the heparin ligand inserts (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Eight residues of dp12 are visible in the electron density map of the G6b-B–dp12–Fab complex.
source: Crystallization involved a dodeca-saccharide, of which eight residues are visible in the electron density map (Figure 6—figure supplement 1), with the central residues 4 and 5 representing sulfated L-iduronic acid (IDS) and D-glucosamine (SGN), respectively.
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: Only one sulfate group (residue SGN5) forms ionic interactions with basic side-chains in the G6b-B–heparin complex.
source: Although the ligand-binding cleft provides partial charge complementarity to the sulfate groups of the heparin ligand (Figure 6A), perhaps surprisingly, only one sulfate group (residue SGN5) forms ionic interactions with basic side-chains (SGN5-O2S – Arg60F-Nε 3.3 Å, SGN5-O3S– Lys109F-Nζ 3.2 Å, where the superscript refers to the chain ID; Figure 6B,C).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 6B,C.

claim: There is exquisite shape complementarity between the heparin and the surface of the G6b-B dimer.
source: There is exquisite shape complementarity between the heparin and the surface of the G6b-B dimer, even though the S-shaped ligand only partially fills the ligand-binding cleft.
evidence: This is stated in the results based on structural analysis.

claim: Heparin bound to both monomeric and dimeric G6b-B with high affinity (low nanomolar range) in SPR experiments.
source: In the configuration with chip-immobilized G6b-B molecules, heparin bound to both monomeric and dimeric G6b-B with high affinity (low nanomolar range).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Table 3.

claim: Fractionated (9 kDa) HS bound to G6b-B with similar affinity to heparin in SPR experiments.
source: Similar values were obtained for fractionated (9 kDa) HS and the 12 saccharide heparin oligomer dp12.
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Table 3.

claim: The binding affinity of perlecan to G6b-B was 366-fold weaker than that of heparin, in the low micromolar range.
source: The binding affinity of perlecan was 366-fold weaker than that of heparin, in the low micromolar range (Table 3 and Figure 7A).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Table 3 and Figure 7A.

claim: In the ligand-immobilized configuration, the binding of monomeric G6b-B was approximately 100-fold weaker than that of the dimer for both heparin and fractionated HS.
source: Interestingly, in the ligand-immobilized configuration, differences in the binding of monomeric and dimeric G6b-B were observed for both heparin and fractionated HS, with the binding of the monomer being approximately 100-fold weaker than that of the dimer (Table 3 and Figure 7B).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Table 3 and Figure 7B.

claim: Heparin and HS both enhanced platelet aggregation in response to subthreshold concentrations of collagen.
source: Heparin and HS both enhanced platelet aggregation in response to subthreshold concentrations of collagen (Figure 11).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 11.

claim: Perlecan did not have an effect on collagen-mediated platelet aggregation at the concentrations tested.
source: We did not find an effect of perlecan on collagen-mediated platelet aggregation at the concentrations tested, suggesting that perlecan must be immobilized to surface in order to provide HS chains at a sufficient density to observe the inhibitory effects observed in adhesion experiments (Figures 8 and 9).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 11.

claim: APAC dose-dependently inhibited collagen-induced platelet aggregation.
source: In contrast to single-chain heparin, APAC dose-dependently inhibited collagen-induced platelet aggregation (Figure 11), with an almost complete block observed at 0.5 µM, as previously described (Lassila and Jouppila, 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 11.

claim: APAC induced robust integrin activation and platelet secretion in G6b-B deficient platelets.
source: APAC and heparin had no detectable effect on WT platelets, but APAC induced robust integrin activation and platelet secretion in G6b-B deficient platelets, demonstrating a platelet-activating effect of this compound in the absence of G6b-B (Figure 12A).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 12A.

claim: APAC significantly inhibited platelet degranulation in response to CLEC-2 stimulation in WT platelets.
source: APAC, but not heparin, significantly inhibited platelet degranulation and fibrinogen binding in response to CLEC-2 stimulation in WT platelets.
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 12B.

claim: APAC significantly inhibited fibrinogen binding in response to CLEC-2 stimulation in WT platelets.
source: APAC, but not heparin, significantly inhibited platelet degranulation and fibrinogen binding in response to CLEC-2 stimulation in WT platelets.
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 12B.

claim: The inhibitory effect of APAC on degranulation was not observed in platelets from G6b-B-deficient animals.
source: Importantly, this inhibitory effect of APAC on degranulation was not observed in platelets from G6b-B-deficient animals (Figure 12B).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 12B.

claim: The inhibitory effect of APAC was absent in the platelets from Mpig6bdiY/F mice.
source: The inhibitory effect of APAC was also absent in the platelets from Mpig6bdiY/F mice, which express a signaling-incompetent form of G6b-B (Figure 12C).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 12C.

claim: APAC suppresses CLEC-2-mediated platelet activation via G6b-B by recruiting the downstream phosphates Shp1 and Shp2.
source: Hence, we conclude that APAC suppresses CLEC-2-mediated platelet activation via G6b-B by recruiting the downstream phosphates Shp1 and Shp2.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data in Figure 12.

claim: Heparin and APAC induced moderate changes in whole-cell tyrosine phosphorylation in washed human platelets.
source: Both heparin or APAC induced moderate changes in whole-cell tyrosine phosphorylation as compared to collagen, with APAC having a stronger effect (Figure 13A).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 13A.

claim: Heparin and APAC enhanced the basal phosphorylation of G6b-B.
source: Heparin, and to a greater extent APAC, enhanced the basal phosphorylation of G6b-B, which was accompanied by an increase in Shp1 and Shp2 association (Figure 13A and Figure 13—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 13A and Figure 13—figure supplement 1.

claim: Heparin and APAC increased Shp1 and Shp2 association with G6b-B.
source: Heparin, and to a greater extent APAC, enhanced the basal phosphorylation of G6b-B, which was accompanied by an increase in Shp1 and Shp2 association (Figure 13A and Figure 13—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 13A and Figure 13—figure supplement 1.

claim: APAC induced prominent phosphorylation of Shp1 (pTyr562) and Shp2 (p-Tyr580 and p-Tyr542).
source: Strikingly, APAC induced prominent phosphorylation of Shp1 and Shp2, whereas heparin only induced modest changes in Shp2 phosphorylation (Figure 13B).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 13B.

claim: Heparin only induced modest changes in Shp2 phosphorylation.
source: Strikingly, APAC induced prominent phosphorylation of Shp1 and Shp2, whereas heparin only induced modest changes in Shp2 phosphorylation (Figure 13B).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 13B.

claim: APAC treatment of WT platelets increased Shp1 and Shp2 phosphorylation.
source: APAC treatment of WT platelets recapitulated the effects observed in human platelets, showing only a modest change in overall phosphorylation pattern, and an increase in Shp1 and Shp2 phosphorylation (Figure 13C,D).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 13C,D.

claim: APAC-induced robust tyrosine phosphorylation in G6b-B-deficient platelets.
source: By contrast, APAC-induced robust tyrosine phosphorylation in G6b-B-deficient platelets (Figure 13C), indicative of reduced inhibitory signaling and platelet hyperreactivity the absence of G6b-B.
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 13C.

claim: APAC treatment resulted in reduced tyrosine phosphorylation of Shp1 and Shp2 in G6b-B-deficient platelets compared with WT platelets.
source: Strikingly, this was accompanied by reduced tyrosine phosphorylation of Shp1 and Shp2 in these platelets compared with WT platelets (Figure 13D).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 13D.

claim: Perlecan inhibited the adhesion of platelets to collagen and fibrinogen.
source: Importantly, co-coating of fibrinogen together with perlecan reduced the adhesion of WT but not of G6b–/–platelets, resulting in enhanced adhesion of Mpig6b–/–platelets under this condition.
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 8B.

claim: The G6b-B–HS interaction inhibited the adhesion of human platelets to the perlecan protein core, collagen and fibrinogen.
source: Collectively, these findings demonstrate that the G6b-B–HS interaction inhibited the adhesion of human platelets to the perlecan protein core, collagen and fibrinogen, suggesting an inhibitory effect on integrin and GPVI signaling.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the adhesion assay data in Figure 8.

claim: Human platelets adhering to fibrinogen exhibited characteristic spreading and actin stress fiber formation.
source: In contrast to human platelets adhering to fibrinogen, which exhibited characteristic spreading and actin stress fiber formation, platelets adhering to perlecan were small in size and did not spread.
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 8C.

claim: Human platelets adhering to perlecan were small in size and did not spread.
source: In contrast to human platelets adhering to fibrinogen, which exhibited characteristic spreading and actin stress fiber formation, platelets adhering to perlecan were small in size and did not spread.
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 8C.

claim: Mpig6b–/–platelets spread to a greater extent on perlecan than WT platelets.
source: Mouse WT platelets, like human platelets, did not spread on perlecan and were small (Figure 8D), although platelets from Mpig6b–/–mice spread to a greater extent, indicating their activation.
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 8D.

claim: G6b-B signaling is required to inhibit platelet activation in the presence of HS.
source: Hence, we conclude that G6b-B signaling is required to inhibit platelet activation in the presence of HS.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the platelet adhesion and spreading data in Figure 8.

claim: Perlecan is expressed in vessel walls in mouse bone marrow sections.
source: Staining of WT mouse bone marrow sections revealed perlecan expression in vessel walls, which co-localized with the sinusoid marker endoglin (CD105) (Figure 9A and Figure 9—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 9A and Figure 9—figure supplement 1.

claim: Perlecan co-localized with the sinusoid marker endoglin (CD105) in mouse bone marrow sections.
source: Staining of WT mouse bone marrow sections revealed perlecan expression in vessel walls, which co-localized with the sinusoid marker endoglin (CD105) (Figure 9A and Figure 9—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 9A and Figure 9—figure supplement 1.

claim: An increased number of MKs was observed in Mpig6b–/–animals.
source: Consistent with previous findings (Mazharian et al., 2012), however, we observed an increased number of MKs in Mpig6b–/–animals (Figure 9B), distributed throughout the bone marrow as atypical clusters (Figure 9C and Figure 9—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 9B.

claim: Mpig6b–/–mice showed similar frequencies of the different maturation stages of MKs as WT mice.
source: Despite the increase in the number of MKs, Mpig6b–/–mice showed similar frequencies of the different maturation stages of MKs, as quantified by EM (Figure 9D,E), arguing against an overall defect of MK maturation in Mpig6b–/–mice.
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 9D,E.

claim: Mpig6b–/–MKs spread to a greater degree on perlecan than WT MKs.
source: We found that only very few WT and Mpig6b–/–MKs adhered to a perlecan-coated surface (Figure 10). Whilst perlecan-adherent WT MKs were small in size, Mpig6b–/–MKs spread to a greater degree on the same substrate.
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 10.

claim: Exposure of MKs to HS resulted in increased size in the absence of G6b-B.
source: Hence, similar to platelets, exposure of MKs to HS resulted in increased size in the absence of G6b-B, confirming the inhibitory function of this receptor.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the MK adhesion data in Figure 10.

claim: Multivalent G6b-B ligands inhibit platelet activation via (hemi)ITAM receptors.
source: Overall, these findings demonstrate that multivalent G6b-B ligands inhibit platelet activation via (hemi)ITAM receptors, whereas soluble single-chain molecules do not.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the aggregation and flow cytometry data in Figures 11 and 12.

claim: Soluble single-chain heparin and HS do not inhibit platelet activation via (hemi)ITAM receptors.
source: Overall, these findings demonstrate that multivalent G6b-B ligands inhibit platelet activation via (hemi)ITAM receptors, whereas soluble single-chain molecules do not.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the aggregation and flow cytometry data in Figures 11 and 12.

claim: To induce robust inhibitory biological or signaling effects, G6b-B ligands need to be either immobilized to a surface or multivalent.
source: Our data demonstrates that, to induce robust inhibitory biological or signaling effects, G6b-B ligands need to be either immobilized to a surface, as in the case of perlecan-coated plates, or multivalent, as in the case of APAC.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the functional assays and signaling data.

claim: Heparin fails to cluster G6b-B sufficiently into higher-order oligomers to induce robust downstream signaling.
source: On the basis of our signaling data and size-exclusion chromatography data, we assume that heparin, despite being able to dimerize the receptor, fails to cluster G6b-B sufficiently into higher-order oligomers to induce robust downstream signaling (Figure 14A,B).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the signaling and biophysical data.

claim: Clustering of G6b-B receptor dimers into higher-order oligomers by an immobilized or multivalent ligand is required for the inhibitory effect on platelet function.
source: We therefore conclude that clustering of G6b-B receptor dimers into higher-order oligomers by an immobilized or multivalent ligand is required for the inhibitory effect on platelet function (Figure 14C).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the functional and signaling data.

claim: Perlecan is secreted by endothelial and smooth muscle cells into the extracellular space of the vessel wall.
source: Perlecan is secreted by endothelial and smooth muscle cells into the extracellular space of the vessel wall and hence is inaccessible by platelet G6b-B in an intact blood vessel (Murdoch et al., 1994; Saku and Furthmayr, 1989; Segev et al., 2004).
evidence: This is a statement supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Perlecan is inaccessible by platelet G6b-B in an intact blood vessel.
source: Perlecan is secreted by endothelial and smooth muscle cells into the extracellular space of the vessel wall and hence is inaccessible by platelet G6b-B in an intact blood vessel (Murdoch et al., 1994; Saku and Furthmayr, 1989; Segev et al., 2004).
evidence: This is inferred from the location of perlecan secretion.

claim: The interaction of platelet G6b-B with perlecan occurs upon vascular injury.
source: Only upon vascular injury will the interaction between platelet G6b-B and perlecan occur, resembling the interaction of other platelet receptors with ligands that are expressed in the vessel wall, including collagen, laminin and fibronectin (Bergmeier and Hynes, 2012).
evidence: This is inferred from the location of perlecan and the context of vascular injury.

claim: The interaction of platelet G6b-B with perlecan negatively regulates the initial steps of thrombus formation.
source: Given the results of our adhesion assay, we speculate that the interaction of platelet G6b-B with perlecan negatively regulates the initial steps of thrombus formation, preventing thrombi from forming unnecessarily.
evidence: This is speculation based on the adhesion assay results.

claim: G6b-B is highly expressed in mature MKs.
source: G6b-B is highly expressed in mature MKs and G6b-B KO and loss-of-function mice show a severe macrothrombocytopenia resulting from impaired proplatelet formation and platelet production, which is accompanied by an increase in MK numbers in the bone marrow (Geer et al., 2018; Mazharian et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a statement supported by citations to previous work.

claim: G6b-B KO and loss-of-function mice show a severe macrothrombocytopenia resulting from impaired proplatelet formation and platelet production.
source: G6b-B is highly expressed in mature MKs and G6b-B KO and loss-of-function mice show a severe macrothrombocytopenia resulting from impaired proplatelet formation and platelet production, which is accompanied by an increase in MK numbers in the bone marrow (Geer et al., 2018; Mazharian et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a statement supported by citations to previous work.

claim: G6b-B-deficient MKs have no overt maturation defect in vitro and ex vivo.
source: Because it has been shown in vitro (Mazharian et al., 2012) and ex vivo (this publication) that G6b-B-deficient MKs have no overt maturation defect and as an increase in size was only observed in the presence of the HS chains of perlecan, it seems unlikely that the increase in size results from an overall maturation defect of the MKs.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and supported by data in this study and a previous citation.

claim: Perlecan is abundantly expressed in the bone marrow ECM and comes into contact with mature MKs.
source: In addition, findings from our study and others demonstrate that perlecan is abundantly expressed in the bone marrow ECM and comes into contact with mature MKs (Farach-Carson et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and supported by data in this study and a previous citation.

claim: The MK G6b-B-HS interaction might play a role in regulating polarized proplatelet formation in the sinusoidal blood vessel lumen.
source: We hypothesize that the MK G6b-B-HS interaction might play a role in regulating polarized proplatelet formation in the sinusoidal blood vessel lumen.
evidence: This is a hypothesis stated in the discussion.

claim: Platelets and MKs from G6b-B-deficient mice showed an activation response towards the HS chains of immobilized perlecan.
source: Moreover, our results also demonstrate that platelets and MKs from G6b-B-deficient mice showed an activation response towards the HS chains of immobilized perlecan and, in case of platelets, also towards APAC, even in the absence of a classical platelet agonist such as collagen.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and supported by data in Figures 8, 10, and 12.

claim: One of the key functions of G6b-B in vivo may be to retain platelets in a resting state by inhibiting other HS-binding platelet receptors.
source: Hence, one of the key functions of G6b-B in vivo may not be solely restricted to the inhibition of platelet function upon vascular injury, but may also retain platelets in a resting state by inhibiting other HS-binding platelet receptors, which remain to be identified.
evidence: This is speculation stated in the discussion.

claim: The HSPGs syndecan-1 and −4 are expressed on the surface of endothelial cells that form an integral part of the glycocalyx.
source: Notably, the HSPGs syndecan-1 and −4 are expressed on the surface of endothelial cells that form an integral part of the glycocalyx (Marki et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a statement supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: The interaction of G6b-B on circulating platelets within the glycocalyx may induce a low level inhibitory signal that helps to maintain platelets in an inactive state.
source: As platelets marginate to the vessel wall, the interaction of G6b-B on circulating platelets within the glycocalyx may induce a low level inhibitory signal that helps to maintain platelets in an inactive state, in line with the basal phosphorylation of G6b-B in resting platelets.
evidence: This is speculation stated in the discussion.
